how much air should i put
documents.overview: Tires affect grip, handling, and stopping. Use the vehicle placard and owner's manual for recommended cold pressure and rotation guidance; the maximum pressure on a tire sidewall is not the vehicle's target pressure.
possible_causes: Pressure loss, wear, alignment or suspension condition, loading, and usage can affect tire condition.
symptoms: Pressure warning, visible damage, low pressure, uneven wear, vibration, or reduced wet-road grip.
checks: Check cold pressure against the vehicle placard/manual and inspect for damage.
Use a suitable tread-depth gauge or have tires inspected.
Do not drive on a visibly damaged, bulging, or rapidly deflating tire.
documents.urgency: A bulge, exposed cords, rapid pressure loss, or tire damage can cause loss of control. Stop safely and arrange assistance.
needed_information: Vehicle, tire size, measured cold pressure, tread measurement, damage, and loading.

sources.name: NHTSA Tire Safety
sources.reference: Official tire safety information.

sources.name: Vehicle tire placard and owner's manual
sources.reference: Use the pressure and maintenance guidance for the exact vehicle.

documents.answer: Correct tire pressure and enough tread are essential for grip, braking and steering. Check the pressures at least once a month with the tires cold, using the figures on the door-jamb sticker or in the owner's manual.
key_causes: slow leaks from punctures or valves
uneven wear from wrong pressure or misalignment
actions: Inflate to the vehicle's placard pressure, not the maximum printed on the tire.
Check the tread-wear indicators and look for cuts, bulges or uneven wear.
Rotate the tires at the interval in the owner's manual.
documents.stop: Replace a tire with a bulge, a deep cut, or tread worn down to the wear indicators.

documents.title: Steering, alignment, suspension, and wheel-bearing symptoms
documents.overview: Steering and suspension symptoms affect vehicle control. Pulling, vibration, or noise can also arise from tires, brakes, road conditions, or wheel alignment.
possible_causes: Tire pressure or wear, alignment, worn suspension joints, shocks/struts, wheel bearings, or brake drag may contribute.
symptoms: Pulling, wandering, excessive bounce, clunks, vibration, uneven tire wear, or humming that changes with speed.
checks: Check tire condition and pressure only when safe.
Have steering, suspension, wheel attachment, and alignment inspected; do not work under an unsupported vehicle.
documents.urgency: Loose steering, a damaged wheel/tire, severe pulling, or a sudden change in handling is safety-critical. Stop safely and arrange inspection.
needed_information: Vehicle, speed and road conditions, recent impacts or repairs, tire condition, noises, and warning lights.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Inspection procedures and alignment specifications are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: Steering and suspension problems show up as clunks over bumps, a wandering or loose feel, uneven tire wear, a humming wheel bearing or the car pulling.
key_causes: worn ball joints, tie-rod ends or bushings
actions: Note when it happens: over bumps, when turning, or at certain speeds.
Check the tire pressures and look for uneven tire wear.
documents.stop: If the steering feels loose or unpredictable, or there's a sudden loud noise, stop driving and have it inspected.
documents.professional: Steering and suspension joints need to be checked on a lift by a technician.
documents.drive_safety: If the steering feels loose or unpredictable, no. Clunks or noises without a change in steering feel should still be inspected soon.

documents.title: Battery, alternator, starter, and charging-system problems
keywords: one click and will not crank
loose ground causes intermittent electrical problems
what does a starter motor do
what does a car battery do
documents.overview: Starting and charging symptoms can involve the battery, starter, alternator, wiring, connections, or another electrical load. A symptom alone cannot identify which part has failed.
component_functions: The battery stores electrical energy for starting and vehicle loads.
The starter motor turns the engine during starting.
The alternator supplies electrical power and charges the battery while the engine runs in vehicles equipped with one.
possible_causes: Low battery charge or capacity, loose/corroded connections, charging-system faults, starter issues, or parasitic electrical draw.
symptoms: Slow crank, clicking, dimming lights, battery/charging warning, repeated jump-start need, or stalling.
checks: Record warning lights and whether the problem occurs after the vehicle sits or while running.
Have battery and charging system tested with appropriate equipment.
Avoid shorting battery terminals; follow the manual for jump-starting.
documents.urgency: A burning smell, smoke, hot wiring, or repeated stalling requires stopping safely and qualified assistance.
needed_information: Battery age, starting behavior, warning lights, recent jump starts, and test results if available.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: Jump-start locations and procedures vary by vehicle.

documents.answer: A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.
key_causes: something draining the battery while parked
a failing starter motor or relay
actions: Rapid clicking with dim lights usually points to a weak battery or poor connection; a single click with bright lights can point to the starter.
With the engine off, check that the battery terminals are tight and free of corrosion.
Jump-start only as the owner's manual describes, then have the battery and charging system tested.
documents.stop: If you smell burning or see smoke from the wiring or battery, stop trying to start the car.
documents.drive_safety: If the car starts and runs normally after a jump-start, you can usually drive it to have the battery and charging system tested. If a charging warning light comes on, stop somewhere safe.

condition_hints.lights: Bright lights mean the battery still has some charge, so a poor battery connection or a starter-motor or relay fault is more likely than a flat battery.
condition_hints.battery: A new battery can still be discharged or poorly connected, so check that the terminals are clean and tight; if they are, a starter-motor or relay fault is the next most likely cause.

triage.ask: When you turn the key, what happens: a rapid clicking, one click, slow cranking, or nothing at all?

answers.narrow: Rapid clicking almost always means a flat battery or a poor connection: there isn't enough power to turn the starter. Try a jump start and check the terminals for looseness or white/green corrosion.
A single click with bright dashboard lights points to the starter motor or its solenoid. Tapping the starter while someone turns the key sometimes gets it going once, but it needs replacing.
Slow cranking means a weak battery, corroded terminals or a tired starter. Have the battery load-tested first; most batteries last about 2 to 4 years in a hot climate.
Nothing at all, with no dashboard lights, means no power reaching the car: a completely flat battery, a loose or corroded main terminal, or a blown main fuse.

triage.ask: Do the dashboard lights and headlights come on brightly?

answers.narrow: Dim lights confirm the battery is low. If it's flat again after a jump and a drive, test the alternator too: it may not be charging.
Bright lights mean the battery has some charge, so the starter, its connection or the ignition switch is more likely than the battery.

documents.title: Dashboard warning lights and OBD diagnostic trouble codes
keywords: P0300 code does not prove spark plugs are bad
does diagnostic code P0300 prove the spark plugs are bad
documents.overview: An OBD diagnostic trouble code identifies a detected condition or circuit that needs diagnosis; it does not automatically identify a failed part. A code reader's description is not a complete diagnosis.
possible_causes: The same code can have multiple causes, including wiring, connections, leaks, sensor readings, or a component fault.
symptoms: Warning lamp, stored or pending code, drivability change, or emissions-related notice.
checks: Record exact codes and freeze-frame data before clearing them.
Follow the vehicle-specific diagnostic procedure and verify the underlying cause before replacing parts.
Use the owner's manual for warning severity.
documents.urgency: A flashing warning, oil-pressure or temperature warning, brake/steering warning, or severe drivability problem needs immediate attention. Do not treat all dashboard lights as equal.
needed_information: Exact code including prefix, warning icon, vehicle make/model/year/engine, and symptoms.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information
sources.reference: Code definitions and diagnostic tests vary by make, model, engine, and year.

documents.answer: Warning lights mean a system needs attention. Red lights (oil pressure, temperature, brakes, charging) usually mean stop soon; amber lights such as the check-engine light mean get it checked soon.
key_causes: a fault detected by one of the car's control modules
actions: Have the diagnostic trouble codes read; a code shows which system or test failed, not which part to replace.
Look up the exact symbol in the owner's manual.
documents.stop: If a red warning appears or the car behaves abnormally, stop safely and check the owner's manual before continuing.

triage.ask: Is the light steady or flashing, and does the car drive normally?

answers.narrow: A flashing engine light means an active misfire that can damage the catalytic converter. Reduce speed and have it checked before driving far.
A steady light with normal driving is usually not urgent. The commonest causes are a loose fuel cap, an oxygen sensor or a small leak in the evaporative system. Have the code read so you know which.

documents.title: Coolant, brake, transmission, and other fluid leaks
keywords: coolant color does not prove compatibility
documents.overview: Fluid color or location alone is not reliable proof of fluid type or source. Some vehicles use different fluids or do not have a serviceable reservoir for a particular system.
possible_causes: A seal, hose, connection, reservoir, or component may leak; fluid can travel before dripping.
symptoms: Puddle, falling fluid level, odor, warning light, overheating, or changed brake/steering/transmission behavior.
checks: Do not taste or touch unknown fluid; keep people and pets away.
Do not open a hot cooling system.
A brake-fluid leak or changed pedal feel requires stopping safely; identify the source professionally.
documents.urgency: Fuel, brake-fluid, major coolant, or oil-pressure-related leaks can be hazardous. Stop safely and seek qualified assistance rather than continuing to drive.
needed_information: Leak location, approximate amount, warning lights, fluid level only if safe to check, and recent service.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: Fluid types, reservoirs, and safe checks are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: Fluid under the car can be coolant, engine oil, brake fluid, transmission or power-steering fluid, or just water from the air-conditioning.
key_causes: a leaking hose, radiator or water pump (coolant)
a leaking brake line or caliper (brake fluid)
normal condensation from the A/C (clear water)
actions: Put a light-coloured sheet under the car overnight to see where it drips and what colour it is.
Check the fluid levels with the engine off and cool.
documents.stop: A brake-fluid or fuel leak, or any leak with a warning light, means don't drive the car; arrange a tow.

documents.title: Filters, spark plugs, and routine preventive service
keywords: clogged fuel filter causes poor performance
do all cars have the same spark plug replacement interval
what does an air filter do
documents.overview: Filters and ignition items have different service requirements. Dust, operating conditions, engine design, and the manufacturer's schedule can change inspection or replacement timing.
component_functions: The engine air filter limits intake contaminants.
The cabin air filter cleans air entering the passenger compartment where fitted.
A fuel filter removes specified contaminants from fuel where the vehicle has a serviceable filter.
possible_causes: A restricted or damaged filter or worn ignition component may affect operation, but symptoms are not enough to confirm the part is due.
symptoms: Reduced airflow, odor, rough running, or a service reminder may prompt inspection but do not determine a universal interval.
checks: Use the schedule for the exact make/model/year/engine and severe-use conditions.
Record completed service and parts used.
Do not set a generic interval as overdue without the applicable schedule and service history.
documents.urgency: Routine service is generally planned maintenance; address warning lights, misfires, or unsafe symptoms promptly.
needed_information: Vehicle identity, engine, mileage, operating conditions, and dated service records.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific maintenance schedule
sources.reference: Use the manufacturer's schedule; no universal interval is asserted here.

documents.answer: Air, cabin and fuel filters, spark plugs and other wear items are replaced at intervals set by the vehicle maker, by distance or time.
actions: Follow the maintenance schedule in the owner's manual or service booklet.
Replace the engine air filter sooner if you drive in dusty conditions.
Keep the service records so you know what was done and when.

documents.title: Mileage-based and time-based maintenance schedules
keywords: what maintenance is overdue at 60000 kilometers
calculate next service date without maintenance history
documents.overview: Maintenance may be scheduled by time, mileage, operating conditions, or a vehicle's monitoring system. Without the applicable maker schedule and verified service records, overdue status cannot be calculated reliably.
possible_causes: Missing history, incorrect mileage, severe operating conditions, or use of the wrong vehicle schedule can make a due-date estimate unreliable.
symptoms: A service reminder or missing record is a reason to check documentation, not proof that a particular component has failed.
checks: Compare dated service records and odometer readings with the exact vehicle's official schedule.
Use manufacturer severe-use guidance where applicable.
Record future due items only after verifying the schedule.
documents.urgency: Safety-related warnings or obvious defects require immediate inspection independent of routine intervals.
needed_information: Exact make/model/year/engine, current odometer, last service dates and odometer, and operating conditions.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and maintenance schedule
sources.reference: No generic mileage or time interval should replace the manufacturer's schedule.

documents.answer: Maintenance schedules are based on both distance and time, whichever comes first. If a service is overdue, book it soon and check whether safety items such as brakes or tires were due.
actions: Compare the odometer and the date of the last service with the schedule in the owner's manual.
Don't skip safety-related items: brakes, tires, steering and fluid checks.

documents.title: Pre-rental and post-rental vehicle inspection
documents.overview: A fleet release inspection is a documented condition check, not a substitute for scheduled service or mechanical diagnosis.
possible_causes: Missed damage, warning lights, tire concerns, incomplete records, or unresolved reported symptoms can be overlooked without a consistent checklist.
symptoms: New damage, warning indicators, abnormal noises, fluid leaks, tire concerns, or customer-reported symptoms.
checks: Record exterior/interior condition, warning lights, tires, visible leaks, mileage, fuel/charge level, and required equipment.
Review open maintenance work and service due status against verified records.
Do not release a vehicle with unresolved safety-critical concerns.
documents.urgency: Brake, steering, tire, severe overheating, oil-pressure, fuel-leak, or other safety-critical concerns require removing the vehicle from service until qualified inspection.
needed_information: Vehicle ID, dated inspection, odometer, checklist results, open work orders, and service schedule.

sources.name: Fleet inspection policy and vehicle-specific owner's manual
sources.reference: The operator should define a documented checklist and follow the manufacturer's requirements.

documents.answer: Before and after each rental, walk around the car and record its condition: body damage, tires, lights, warning lights, fuel level and mileage.
actions: Take dated photos of all sides, the wheels, the interior, the odometer and the fuel gauge.
Check the tires, lights and wipers, and that no warning lights stay on after starting.
Report any damage or fault to the rental team before driving off.
documents.stop: Don't drive or rent out a car with a safety-related fault such as damaged tires, a brake warning or faulty lights.

documents.title: Vehicle health assessment and missing diagnostic information
keywords: confirm car is safe based only on mileage
which parts of this rental vehicle should be inspected first
what parts should I inspect first
model score prove vehicle has no faults
reported symptoms versus technician confirmed faults
confirm vehicle passed inspection when no inspection record was supplied
documents.overview: A reliable health assessment combines verified vehicle identity, mileage, service history, inspection findings, and relevant diagnostic measurements. A short chat description or model score cannot establish overall vehicle condition.
possible_causes: Incomplete history, missing measurements, unverified user reports, or a model trained on different data can limit an assessment.
symptoms: A symptom should be recorded with when it occurs, warning indicators, and any inspection or scan results.
checks: Separate recorded facts, user-reported symptoms, model recommendations, and technician-confirmed faults.
Prioritize safety-critical symptoms for inspection.
Request make/model/year/engine, mileage, warning codes, service history, and symptom conditions.
documents.urgency: A low model score cannot establish that a vehicle is safe. Safety-critical symptoms must be addressed independently of model output.
needed_information: Vehicle identity, current mileage, service records, warning codes, inspection results, and symptom details.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information and verified fleet records
sources.reference: A model can use only the inputs and targets it was trained and validated to support.

documents.answer: Inspect the safety items first: tires, brakes, steering, lights and any warning lights, then anything the service history shows is due. A vehicle-health assessment is only as good as its data and can't confirm a part's condition on its own.
actions: Record inspections, odometer readings and repairs consistently.
Use the assessment to decide what to inspect, not as a diagnosis.
documents.stop: A low model score cannot establish that a vehicle is safe; deal with brake, steering, tire or warning-light problems regardless of the model output.

documents.title: Interpreting maintenance model recommendations and scores
keywords: low model score prove vehicle is safe
documents.overview: A model recommendation is a statistical signal based on its training labels and supplied features. It is not a confirmed defect, calibrated failure probability, remaining useful life, or prediction of a failure date.
possible_causes: Scores may reflect patterns in training data and are limited by training coverage, feature quality, label quality, and the configured decision threshold.
symptoms: A flagged category means the model crossed its configured recommendation threshold; a low score does not prove that the vehicle is fault-free.
checks: Review the supplied feature values, threshold, service history, and a physical inspection.
Explain the model's actual recorded output; never infer a failed part or invent a probability.
documents.urgency: Use safety-critical symptoms and qualified inspection to determine immediate action; do not use model output alone to declare a vehicle safe.
needed_information: The model response, supplied features, model version, threshold, and relevant inspection/history data.

sources.name: Local maintenance model artifact and evaluation report
sources.reference: Use only outputs that the installed artifact actually returns; confirm limitations against its evaluation.

documents.answer: The maintenance model's score shows how closely a vehicle's data resembles past cases that needed service. It's a prompt to inspect, not a confirmed fault.
actions: Use high-scoring vehicles to prioritise inspections.
Confirm any recommendation with a physical inspection before ordering repairs.

documents.title: Fleet maintenance prioritization and recurring issues
documents.overview: Fleet comparisons require authorized, comparable vehicle records and service history. A model can rank only the eligible records actually supplied to it.
possible_causes: Missing mileage, stale inspections, inconsistent labels, and incomplete maintenance history can distort prioritization or hide recurring issues.
symptoms: Repeated work orders, safety-critical findings, overdue verified service, and model recommendations are distinct evidence types and should be reported separately.
checks: Compare dated records with vehicle-specific schedules.
Prioritize confirmed safety defects and urgent symptoms before routine predictive recommendations.
Report analyzed, rejected, and missing records rather than treating missing data as low risk.
documents.urgency: Do not infer that an unreported vehicle has no maintenance need; flag missing or stale records for follow-up.
needed_information: Authorized fleet records, vehicle identities, mileage, service dates, inspection findings, and supported model inputs.

sources.name: Authorized fleet maintenance records and vehicle-specific schedules
sources.reference: Fleet conclusions are limited to the records supplied by the authorized backend.

documents.answer: Prioritise fleet maintenance by safety first (brakes, tires, steering, warning lights), then overdue services, then recurring problems.
actions: Take vehicles with safety-related faults out of service until they're repaired.
Track recurring problems per vehicle to spot repeat faults.
Schedule overdue services before the next booking.

documents.title: Difference between a symptom, diagnostic code, and confirmed fault
keywords: difference between symptom DTC and diagnosis
confirm cause before replacing a part
documents.overview: A symptom is an observed behavior, a diagnostic code is a recorded indication, and a confirmed fault requires appropriate testing or inspection. They should not be presented as interchangeable.
possible_causes: Different faults can create similar symptoms, and one code can have several possible causes.
symptoms: Noise, warning light, vibration, odor, or changed performance are observations to document, not proof of a specific failed component.
checks: Record the condition and exact warning/code.
Use manufacturer diagnostic procedures and confirm findings before repair.
Seek a qualified technician when safety or specialized testing is involved.
documents.urgency: Treat warning lights and safety-critical symptoms according to the owner's manual; severe brake, steering, overheating, oil-pressure, or fuel symptoms require prompt action.
needed_information: Exact vehicle, observed symptom, warning codes, conditions, and test or inspection results.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific service information
sources.reference: Diagnosis requires the correct procedure and supporting test results.

documents.answer: A symptom is what you notice, a diagnostic trouble code shows which test or circuit failed, and a confirmed fault is what an inspection proves. A code alone doesn't tell you which part to replace.
actions: Note the symptoms and read the codes, then confirm the cause by inspection or testing before replacing parts.

documents.title: Hybrid and electric vehicle high-voltage safety
keywords: do hybrids and electric cars use only one coolant circuit
documents.overview: Hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and battery-electric vehicles can contain high-voltage traction circuits in addition to ordinary low-voltage electrical systems. Their layouts, isolation methods, interlocks, stored energy, and technician requirements are vehicle-specific; a symptom or warning does not make exposed components safe to touch.
component_functions: A traction battery stores energy for an electric drive system; a battery-management system monitors and controls it.
An inverter and electric motor convert and use electrical energy; hybrid designs may also include an engine and separate power paths.
Some vehicles have multiple thermal circuits for the traction battery, power electronics, motor, engine, or cabin; one reservoir must not be assumed to serve all circuits.
possible_causes: A warning may relate to low-voltage supply, charging equipment, thermal management, isolation monitoring, battery-management controls, wiring, or a high-voltage component; the displayed message and vehicle-specific diagnostic data are needed.
symptoms: A high-voltage or hybrid-system warning, reduced propulsion, charging interruption, unusual heat, smoke, odor, crash damage, or fluid intrusion warrants cautious handling.
checks: Do not open a traction-battery enclosure, touch orange cables/connectors, probe high-voltage terminals, defeat an interlock, or attempt isolation yourself.
For smoke, fire, unusual heat, crash damage, or hissing/odor, move people away, stop using or charging the vehicle if safe, and contact emergency responders or qualified assistance.
Use only the owner's manual for user-level instructions such as warning response, towing, and charging; do not assume conventional jump-start or fluid-check procedures apply.
diagnostic_steps: A trained high-voltage technician must identify the exact vehicle architecture and follow its manufacturer's isolation, verification, PPE, and service procedures before working on high-voltage components.
Do not infer battery failure from a warning code alone; diagnosis may involve scan data and manufacturer-defined isolation, electrical, thermal, and control-system tests.
professional_diagnostics: High-voltage diagnosis and battery opening require appropriately trained and equipped personnel using exact manufacturer service information; this knowledge base does not provide an isolation procedure.
vehicle_variations: Battery-electric, hybrid, and plug-in hybrid architectures differ; even vehicles of the same make may have different battery, inverter, charging, and thermal layouts by year and trim.
known_unknowns: No make, model, year, warning message, or service document was supplied, so no component-level diagnosis or procedure can be given.
documents.urgency: Do not touch or service exposed high-voltage components. For smoke, fire, unusual heat, collision damage, or electrical hazard, move away and seek emergency or qualified assistance. Do not charge a damaged or abnormally hot vehicle.
needed_information: Make/model/year and powertrain type, exact dashboard message, whether charging or propulsion is affected, and any collision, flooding, smoke, heat, or odor.
documents.source_gap: No exact manufacturer owner or high-voltage service document was supplied or retrieved; only general hazard boundaries are provided.
documents.answer: Hybrid and electric cars use high-voltage systems that can cause a fatal electric shock. Never open, touch or cut the orange high-voltage cables or the battery pack.
actions: Leave high-voltage work to technicians trained and equipped for it.
Follow the owner's manual for warnings, charging and towing.
documents.stop: After a crash, or if you see smoke, smell burning or hear hissing from the battery, move away from the vehicle and call emergency services.
documents.drive_safety: If a high-voltage warning is shown, follow the owner's manual. After a crash, or with smoke or hissing from the battery, don't drive it; move away and call for help.

documents.title: Cabin heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning concerns
keywords: hybrid heater and defroster stopped working
documents.overview: Cabin heating and air-conditioning depend on airflow, heat exchangers, doors and controls, and—in vehicles with conventional A/C—a sealed refrigerant circuit. A warm vent or weak airflow does not by itself identify a failed compressor or refrigerant leak.
component_functions: The blower moves air through cabin filters and heat exchangers.
A heater may use engine coolant, an electric heater, or another vehicle-specific heat source; blend doors route air through the selected path.
Air conditioning transfers cabin heat through a refrigerant circuit with components such as a compressor, condenser, metering device, and evaporator, but architectures vary.
possible_causes: Weak airflow can result from a blower, control, filter, door, or electrical issue.
Warm air with normal airflow can involve control settings, blend-door operation, heat-source availability, refrigerant-circuit performance, or a sensor/control fault.
Odor, water, noise, or intermittent behavior may have several causes and requires inspection.
symptoms: Compare airflow strength at available fan settings, vent temperature, selected mode, outside conditions, and whether the concern affects heating, cooling, or both.
checks: Confirm the selected temperature, fan, recirculation, and outlet settings; consult the vehicle manual for normal operation.
Do not handle refrigerant, loosen A/C fittings, bypass pressure switches, or probe moving/electrically controlled components.
If cabin heat is lost at the same time as engine overheating, treat the engine-temperature warning as urgent and follow the cooling-system safety guidance.
diagnostic_steps: A qualified technician may inspect filters, airflow doors, blower controls, electrical supplies, temperature sensors, and system performance using vehicle-specific procedures.
Refrigerant identification, pressure testing, recovery, leak repair, and charging require suitable equipment and applicable legal/technical procedures; a pressure reading alone is not a diagnosis.
professional_diagnostics: A/C refrigerant service and suspected refrigerant leaks should be handled by appropriately equipped personnel; exact refrigerant and charge specification are vehicle-specific.
vehicle_variations: HVAC controls, refrigerants, heat sources, auxiliary heaters, and multi-zone layouts vary by model; hybrid and electric vehicles may use heat pumps or high-voltage compressors.
known_unknowns: No vehicle identity, refrigerant label, test readings, or manufacturer procedure was supplied; no fluid type, charge amount, pressure, or repair procedure is asserted.
documents.urgency: A cabin comfort fault alone is often not an immediate mechanical emergency, but impaired windshield defrosting, burning odor, smoke, electrical overheating, or concurrent engine overheating requires stopping safely and arranging inspection.
needed_information: Make/model/year, powertrain, heating or cooling complaint, airflow strength, selected mode, warning messages, odors/noises, recent service, and ambient conditions.
documents.source_gap: No exact manufacturer HVAC information or refrigerant service data was available; guidance is limited to general system roles and safe boundaries.
documents.answer: Weak or warm air from the A/C usually comes from low refrigerant, a compressor problem, a blocked cabin filter or condenser, or a blower or control fault.
key_causes: a blocked condenser or a condenser fan that isn't running
a blower motor, resistor or control fault
actions: Check whether air is blowing strongly; weak airflow points to the blower or cabin filter rather than the refrigerant.
Check whether the fan in front of the radiator runs when the A/C is on.
documents.professional: Refrigerant work needs a qualified A/C technician; don't add refrigerant without finding the leak and knowing the correct type.

triage.ask: Is the air warm all the time, or cold at first and then warm, or cold only while driving?

answers.narrow: Warm air all the time usually means low refrigerant from a leak, or the compressor not engaging. Check whether the compressor clutch at the front of the engine spins when the A/C is on.
Cold at first and then warm points to the evaporator freezing up or the compressor cutting out, often from low refrigerant or a faulty pressure switch.
Cold while driving but warm in traffic means the condenser isn't getting air at low speed: a faulty condenser fan or a blocked condenser.

documents.title: Exhaust leaks, emissions controls, and diesel particulate filters
keywords: what does a catalytic converter do
documents.overview: The exhaust system carries combustion gases away and may include oxygen sensors, a catalytic converter, exhaust-gas recirculation, and diesel aftertreatment such as a particulate filter. A warning or code identifies a condition to investigate, not a component proven failed.
component_functions: The catalytic converter uses precious-metal catalysts to turn harmful exhaust gases (carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides) into less harmful ones.
An oxygen sensor reports exhaust-related measurements to the control system; the code or reading does not alone prove sensor failure.
A catalytic converter and, where fitted, a diesel particulate filter treat or capture specified exhaust constituents.
Diesel filter regeneration and EGR operation are managed according to the particular engine and aftertreatment design.
possible_causes: A leak, damaged wiring, sensor circuit, air/fuel issue, engine misfire, exhaust restriction, or aftertreatment operating condition may cause an emissions warning or changed exhaust behavior.
A DPF warning may reflect loading or a system fault; the exact message and manufacturer procedure determine safe next steps.
symptoms: Exhaust odor, ticking or hissing, smoke, reduced power, warning messages, or a scan code can help guide inspection but do not confirm a failed catalyst, sensor, EGR valve, or filter.
checks: If exhaust fumes enter the cabin, stop using the vehicle and get fresh air; carbon monoxide cannot be reliably detected by smell.
Record the exact warning and diagnostic codes, including pending status and freeze-frame data, before clearing anything.
Do not block, remove, bypass, or modify emissions equipment, and do not initiate an unfamiliar regeneration procedure.
diagnostic_steps: A technician may inspect for leaks, review engine and aftertreatment data, verify sensor circuits and plausibility, and follow the exact manufacturer diagnostic tree before parts replacement.
After repair, confirm the fault is corrected and the applicable readiness/monitoring checks complete using the vehicle-specific method.
professional_diagnostics: Exhaust leaks, catalyst/DPF faults, sensor diagnosis, and regeneration procedures require exact vehicle service information and suitable diagnostic equipment.
vehicle_variations: Aftertreatment hardware and regeneration behavior differ by gasoline/diesel engine, model year, market, and duty cycle; motorcycles may use different or simpler exhaust-control systems.
known_unknowns: No exact vehicle, code, exhaust measurement, or warning message was supplied, so no specific component or regeneration procedure can be identified.
documents.urgency: Exhaust fumes in the cabin, smoke, fire risk, severe power loss, or a flashing engine warning requires stopping safely and prompt assistance. Do not run an engine in an enclosed space.
needed_information: Make/model/year, engine and fuel type, exact warning/code, symptoms and operating conditions, recent repairs, and scan/freeze-frame results.
documents.source_gap: No vehicle-specific emissions or aftertreatment service procedure was available; no code-specific definition or regeneration steps are asserted.
documents.answer: Exhaust leaks, emission-control faults and a blocked diesel particulate filter (DPF) can cause loud exhaust noise, fumes, warning lights or reduced power.
key_causes: a leaking exhaust pipe, gasket or manifold
a DPF blocked by short trips
a faulty oxygen or exhaust sensor
actions: Have the codes read if a warning light is on.
For a DPF warning, follow the owner's manual; some cars need a sustained drive to clean the filter.
documents.stop: If you smell exhaust fumes inside the car, open the windows, stop and get out; carbon monoxide is dangerous.
documents.drive_safety: If you smell exhaust fumes inside the car, no. A DPF or emissions warning usually allows careful driving to a workshop; follow the owner's manual.

documents.title: White smoke or steam from the exhaust
documents.overview: Thin white vapour for a few minutes after a cold start, especially in cool or humid weather, is usually water condensation in the exhaust and is normal. Persistent, thick white smoke after the engine is warm, particularly with a sweet smell, can mean coolant is entering the combustion chambers and being burned.
component_functions: The cooling system is sealed from the combustion chambers by the head gasket and the cylinder head and block castings; if that seal fails, coolant can be drawn into the cylinders and leave as white smoke.
possible_causes: A failed head gasket is one possible cause of coolant entering the cylinders.
A cracked or warped cylinder head or cylinder block, often after the engine has overheated.
On some engines, a leaking intake-manifold gasket or EGR cooler can also let coolant reach the cylinders.
On diesel engines, white smoke when cold can also be unburned fuel from faulty glow plugs, injectors, injection timing or low compression.
For comparison: blue-grey smoke usually indicates burning oil, and black smoke usually indicates too much fuel or incomplete combustion.
symptoms: Warning signs that point toward a coolant problem: the coolant level keeps dropping with no visible leak, the engine overheats or the temperature gauge climbs, a sweet smell from the exhaust, bubbles in the coolant reservoir, a milky or creamy residue in the oil, or misfiring after a cold start.
checks: Note the colour and smell of the smoke, whether it continues once the engine is warm, and the temperature gauge reading.
Check the coolant level only when the engine is cold; never open a hot radiator or reservoir cap.
If the engine is overheating or coolant is being lost, stop driving it; continuing can cause severe engine damage.
professional_diagnostics: A technician can pressure-test the cooling system, test the coolant for combustion gases (block test), and run compression or leak-down tests to confirm whether the head gasket, cylinder head or another part is at fault before any repair.
documents.urgency: Brief white vapour on a cold start that clears is normal. Persistent thick white smoke, especially with coolant loss or overheating, needs a prompt professional inspection, and the vehicle should not be driven while it is overheating.
needed_information: Vehicle make, model, year and fuel type, how long the smoke lasts, its colour and smell, coolant level, and any overheating or warning lights.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Cooling-system service and engine diagnosis procedures are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: Thin white vapour that clears once the engine warms up is usually just condensation. Thick white smoke that keeps coming, especially with a sweet smell, can mean coolant is burning in the engine; a failed head gasket is one possible cause.
actions: Check the coolant level with the engine cold.
Watch the temperature gauge.
documents.stop: If the engine starts to overheat or the coolant level keeps dropping, stop driving and have it inspected.
documents.professional: A cooling-system pressure test or combustion-gas test confirms an internal leak.
documents.drive_safety: Thin vapour on a cold start is normal. With thick white smoke, a dropping coolant level or rising temperature, don't keep driving.

documents.title: Motorcycle chain, belt, and shaft final-drive concerns
documents.overview: Many motorcycles use a chain and sprockets, a belt, or a shaft final drive. Wear, lubrication, alignment, tension, and inspection requirements depend on the exact drive design and manufacturer procedure.
component_functions: A chain and sprockets transmit engine torque to the rear wheel and require model-specific inspection and maintenance.
Belt and shaft drives have different inspection and service needs; chain adjustment guidance must not be applied to them.
possible_causes: Noise, tight spots, excess slack, uneven wear, damaged links or teeth, misalignment, lubrication condition, or wheel/drive faults can affect final-drive operation.
symptoms: Clicking, tight spots during wheel rotation, snatch or lash, visible damage, unusual slack, or a change after wheel service warrants inspection.
checks: Do not touch or adjust a moving chain. Keep hands, clothing, and tools away from the drive while the engine is running.
With the motorcycle secured and engine off, perform only the inspection described by its owner's manual; do not assume one slack value applies to all bikes.
Do not ride with a damaged, binding, or visibly unsafe final drive; arrange qualified inspection.
diagnostic_steps: A technician should verify chain/belt/shaft type, wheel alignment, tension or play at the specified measurement point, wear limits, and fastener procedures using the exact model service information.
professional_diagnostics: Adjustment values, lubrication products, wear limits, and axle torque are model-specific and are not provided here.
vehicle_variations: Motorcycle chain, belt, and shaft-drive layouts differ from passenger-car drivetrains; rider load and suspension position may affect specified chain measurement procedure.
known_unknowns: No motorcycle make, model, year, drive type, measured condition, or manual was supplied; no adjustment specification is asserted.
documents.urgency: A damaged or binding motorcycle final drive can cause loss of propulsion or control. Do not ride if the drive appears damaged or unsafe.
needed_information: Motorcycle make/model/year, chain/belt/shaft type, noise or visible damage, inspection findings, recent wheel work, and the manual's specified check.
documents.source_gap: No exact motorcycle owner's or service manual was supplied or retrieved; adjustment values and repair instructions remain unavailable.
documents.answer: Motorcycle chains, belts and shafts need regular inspection, cleaning, lubrication and tension adjustment as the owner's manual specifies.
key_causes: a dry, dirty or stretched chain
actions: With the engine off and the bike secure, check the chain slack and look for tight spots or damaged links.
Adjust and lubricate as the owner's manual describes.
documents.stop: Don't ride with a damaged, binding or very loose chain.

documents.title: Grinding or scraping noise when braking
documents.overview: A grinding or metal-on-metal scraping sound when braking usually means the brake friction material is worn through, so the metal pad backing plate is rubbing the rotor, or something such as a stone is caught between the pad, rotor or dust shield. It can quickly damage the rotors and reduce braking performance.
possible_causes: Brake pads worn down to the backing plate.
A stone or debris trapped between the pad, rotor or dust shield.
Badly worn or scored rotors, or a seized or sticking caliper.
A grinding noise that is also present when not braking can come from a worn wheel bearing.
symptoms: Grinding that gets worse with harder braking, a vibrating pedal, the car pulling to one side when braking, or longer stopping distances.
checks: Treat grinding as urgent: avoid hard braking and limit driving to reaching a safe place or a workshop.
Do not rely on sound alone to judge what is left of the pads; have them and the rotors measured.
professional_diagnostics: A technician removes the wheels to inspect pad thickness, rotor condition and thickness, calipers, slide pins and wheel bearings, and replaces parts against the vehicle's specified limits.
documents.urgency: Have the brakes inspected before driving further. If braking feels weaker, the pedal goes soft, or the car pulls when braking, stop when it is safe and arrange for the vehicle to be inspected or towed.
needed_information: Whether the noise happens only when braking, from which wheel, how long it has been happening, and when the brakes were last serviced.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Brake inspection and wear limits are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: A grinding or metal-on-metal noise when braking usually means the pads are worn through and metal is rubbing the rotor, or something is caught in the brake.
key_causes: pads worn down to the backing plate
a stone or debris caught between the rotor and its shield
a badly worn or damaged rotor
actions: Avoid hard braking and arrange a brake inspection straight away.
documents.stop: Grinding brakes can lose stopping power and quickly damage the rotors: stop using the car and have it inspected or towed.
documents.drive_safety: No. Grinding brakes can lose stopping power and damage the rotors quickly; have the car inspected or towed.

documents.title: Car shakes, shudders or vibrates when braking
documents.overview: Shaking or a pulsing pedal that happens when you brake usually comes from the brakes themselves, most often brake rotors with uneven thickness or uneven pad deposits (often called warped rotors). Worn suspension or steering parts, loose wheel nuts or wheel and tire problems can make it worse.
possible_causes: Uneven rotor thickness or pad material deposits on the rotors.
A sticking caliper or uneven pad wear.
Worn suspension or steering components, or worn wheel bearings.
Loose wheel nuts or a damaged wheel or tire, which can shake at other times too.
ABS pulsing during hard braking on a slippery surface is normal and is not this fault.
symptoms: A steering wheel that shakes when braking points more to the front brakes; a pulsing pedal or seat shake can involve the rear. Shaking that continues without braking points to wheels, tires or suspension.
checks: Note the speed at which it happens and whether it occurs only when braking.
If wheels were recently removed, have the wheel-nut tightness checked before driving far.
professional_diagnostics: A technician measures rotor thickness variation and run-out, checks pads, calipers, wheel nuts, bearings, suspension joints and wheel balance.
documents.urgency: Have it inspected soon. Strong shaking, the car pulling when braking, a loose wheel or reduced braking is safety-critical: stop when it is safe and have the vehicle checked.
needed_information: When it shakes (only when braking, at what speed), where you feel it (steering wheel, pedal, seat), and recent brake or tire work.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Brake rotor limits and suspension checks are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: Shaking or a pulsing pedal when braking usually means the brake rotors are uneven (often called warped), or there's a problem with the wheels, tires or suspension.
key_causes: uneven rotor thickness or deposits on the rotors
loose wheel nuts or wheel imbalance
actions: Note whether you feel it through the pedal or the steering wheel, and at what speed.
Have the rotors measured during a brake inspection.
documents.stop: If the vibration is severe or braking feels weaker, stop driving and have the brakes checked.
documents.drive_safety: Mild vibration isn't an emergency, but have the brakes checked soon. If braking feels weaker or the shaking is severe, stop driving.

triage.ask: Do you feel it through the steering wheel or through the brake pedal?

answers.narrow: Shaking through the steering wheel when braking usually means uneven front discs (often called warped).
A pulsing pedal usually means uneven discs; if it only happens in hard stops with a buzzing pedal, that's normal ABS working.

documents.title: Car pulls or drifts to one side
documents.overview: A car that pulls or drifts to one side most often has uneven tire pressures, uneven tire wear, or a wheel alignment problem. If it pulls only when braking, a sticking brake caliper or uneven braking on one side is more likely.
possible_causes: Low or uneven tire pressure, or tires of different wear or type on the same axle.
Wheel alignment that is out of specification, for example after hitting a pothole or kerb.
A sticking brake caliper or brake hose problem (pulling mainly when braking, sometimes with a hot wheel or burning smell).
Worn or damaged steering or suspension parts.
A road that slopes toward the edge (road crown) can cause a mild drift on some roads only.
symptoms: Note whether it pulls all the time, only when braking, or only on some roads, and whether the steering wheel is off-centre when driving straight.
checks: Check all tire pressures cold against the placard on the door frame and look for uneven wear or damage.
Do not drive on a tire that is damaged or keeps losing pressure.
professional_diagnostics: A technician checks tires, wheel alignment, steering and suspension joints, and brakes for drag on each wheel.
documents.urgency: Correct tire pressure first and have the alignment checked soon. Strong pulling, pulling when braking, loose steering or a damaged tire is safety-critical: stop when it is safe and have the vehicle inspected.
needed_information: When it pulls (always, only when braking, on all roads), which direction, and any recent tire, wheel or suspension work.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Tire pressures and alignment specifications are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: A car that pulls or drifts to one side usually has uneven tire pressure, wheel misalignment, a dragging brake or a worn steering or suspension part.
actions: Check and correct the tire pressures first.
Note whether it pulls all the time or only when braking; pulling only when braking points to the brakes.
documents.stop: If the pull is sudden or strong, or happens when braking, have it inspected before driving further.
documents.drive_safety: A slight pull isn't an emergency, but have it checked soon. A strong or sudden pull, or one only when braking, should be inspected before driving further.

triage.ask: Does it pull all the time, or only when you brake?

answers.narrow: Pulling only when braking points to a sticking caliper or a contaminated pad on one side. Feel the wheels after a drive: the hotter one has the dragging brake.
Pulling all the time is usually uneven tire pressure first, then wheel alignment. Check the pressures on both sides; if they match, have the alignment checked.

documents.title: Flashing (blinking) check-engine light
documents.overview: A flashing (blinking) check-engine light means the engine computer has detected a severe misfire that can overheat and damage the catalytic converter. It is more urgent than a steady check-engine light: reduce speed and load, stop in a safe place as soon as you can, and avoid continued driving.
possible_causes: A severe engine misfire, for example from a failed ignition coil or spark plug, a fuel-delivery problem, or low compression; the exact cause needs a scan and inspection.
symptoms: Shaking or rough running, loss of power, a fuel or sulphur smell, or a hot exhaust can accompany it.
checks: Pull over and stop safely as soon as possible, and switch off the engine if it is running very rough.
Avoid continued driving: if the light keeps flashing when you restart, have the vehicle towed or inspected where it is rather than driving on.
Note any other warning lights, especially temperature or oil pressure.
professional_diagnostics: A technician reads the stored codes and freeze-frame data, finds which cylinder is misfiring and why, and checks the catalytic converter before the car is driven normally again.
documents.urgency: Urgent: stop in a safe place and avoid continued driving until the vehicle is inspected. A steady (not flashing) check-engine light is less urgent but should still be scanned soon.
needed_information: Whether the light is flashing or steady, other warning lights, how the engine is running, and any codes from a scan tool.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Warning-light meanings and required responses vary by vehicle.

documents.answer: A flashing (blinking) check-engine light usually means a severe misfire that can quickly overheat and damage the catalytic converter.
key_causes: a failed spark plug or ignition coil
actions: Have the codes read as soon as possible.
documents.stop: Reduce speed and load, stop in a safe place as soon as you can, and avoid continued driving until the vehicle is inspected or towed.
documents.drive_safety: No. A flashing check-engine light means a severe misfire that can damage the catalytic converter; stop when it's safe and arrange an inspection or a tow.

documents.title: Blue or blue-grey smoke from the exhaust
documents.overview: Blue or blue-grey exhaust smoke usually means engine oil is getting into the combustion chambers and being burned. The engine then uses oil between changes, which can lead to low oil level and can damage the catalytic converter over time.
possible_causes: Worn piston rings or cylinder walls (often more smoke under acceleration).
Worn valve stem seals or valve guides (often a puff of smoke at startup or after idling).
A worn turbocharger seal on turbocharged engines.
A faulty PCV (crankcase ventilation) system, or an engine overfilled with oil.
symptoms: The oil level drops between changes, oily deposits at the tailpipe, fouled spark plugs, or a burning-oil smell.
checks: Check the oil level with the engine off on level ground and top up to the mark if low; do not overfill.
Note when the smoke appears (at startup, when accelerating, after idling).
professional_diagnostics: A technician can check oil consumption, the PCV system and the turbocharger, and run compression or leak-down tests to find where the oil is entering.
documents.urgency: Keep the oil at the correct level and have it inspected soon. Heavy smoke with an oil-pressure warning or very low oil needs you to stop driving.
needed_information: When the smoke appears, how much oil is used between changes, mileage, and whether the engine is turbocharged.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Oil specifications and engine diagnosis are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: Blue or blue-grey exhaust smoke means the engine is burning oil.
key_causes: worn piston rings or valve-stem seals
actions: Check the oil level regularly and top up with the oil grade in the owner's manual.
Have the engine inspected to find where the oil is getting in.
documents.stop: If the oil level drops quickly or the oil-pressure light comes on, stop driving.
documents.drive_safety: Usually for short trips while you arrange a repair, as long as the oil level is kept up. Stop if the oil-pressure light comes on.

documents.title: Black smoke from the exhaust
documents.overview: Black or dark sooty exhaust smoke usually means the engine is burning too much fuel for the air it gets (a rich mixture), so the fuel does not burn completely. On diesel engines a little smoke under hard acceleration can be normal, but persistent black smoke is not.
possible_causes: A clogged engine air filter or restricted air intake.
Leaking or faulty fuel injectors, or a fuel-pressure regulator problem.
A faulty sensor such as the mass airflow, oxygen or coolant-temperature sensor.
On diesels: injector faults, low turbo boost, a stuck EGR valve, or a blocked particulate filter.
symptoms: Higher fuel use, a fuel smell, soot at the tailpipe, reduced power, or a check-engine light.
checks: Check the engine air filter if you can reach it safely.
Note whether the smoke is constant or only under acceleration, and any warning lights.
professional_diagnostics: A technician scans for codes, reviews fuel trims and sensor readings, and checks injectors, intake and boost.
documents.urgency: Usually not an immediate safety risk, but have it diagnosed soon to avoid damage to the catalytic converter or particulate filter. If the check-engine light is flashing, stop driving.
needed_information: Fuel type (gasoline or diesel), when the smoke appears, warning lights, and fuel economy changes.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Fuel-system and emissions diagnosis are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: Black or dark sooty exhaust smoke means the engine is burning too much fuel for the air it gets: a rich mixture.
key_causes: a leaking or sticking fuel injector
a faulty mass-airflow or oxygen sensor
on diesels, a turbo or injector fault
actions: Check the engine air filter.
Have the codes read and the fuel system checked.

documents.title: Steering wheel shakes or vibrates at high speed
keywords: steering wheel shakes at high speed
documents.overview: Shaking that comes through the steering wheel at higher speeds, and is not tied to braking, most often comes from the wheels and tires: a wheel out of balance (for example a lost balance weight), a bent rim, or a damaged or unevenly worn tire. Worn steering or suspension parts and loose wheel nuts can also cause it.
possible_causes: Wheel and tire imbalance, often after a tire change or a lost wheel weight.
A bent wheel rim, or a tire with a bulge, flat spot, separated tread or uneven wear.
Loose wheel nuts, especially after recent wheel work.
Worn tie-rod ends, ball joints, wheel bearings or other steering and suspension parts.
symptoms: Shaking that starts at a certain speed and eases above or below it points to balance; shaking only when braking points to the brakes instead.
checks: Look at each tire for bulges, cuts or uneven wear, and check the tire pressures when cold.
If the wheels were removed recently, have the wheel-nut tightness checked before driving far.
Avoid high speeds until the cause is found.
professional_diagnostics: A technician balances the wheels, checks the rims and tires for damage, and inspects the steering, suspension and wheel bearings.
documents.urgency: Have it inspected soon. A tire bulge, a loose wheel, or shaking that suddenly gets worse is safety-critical: slow down, stop when it is safe and do not continue until it is checked.
needed_information: The speed at which it starts, whether it happens when braking, and recent tire or wheel work.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Tire, wheel and suspension specifications are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: A steering wheel that shakes at higher speeds is most often caused by unbalanced wheels, and sometimes by a damaged tire, a bent wheel or worn steering parts.
key_causes: a tire with a bulge or uneven wear
worn tie-rod ends or suspension parts
actions: Have the wheels balanced and the tires checked for bulges.
Make sure the wheel nuts are tight.
documents.stop: If the vibration is sudden or severe, slow down and stop safely; a tire may be failing.
documents.drive_safety: Keep to lower speeds and have the wheels checked soon. If the vibration is sudden or severe, stop; a tire may be failing.

triage.ask: At what speed does it start, and does it stay the same whether you accelerate or coast?

answers.narrow: A shake that appears around 80 to 100 km/h and doesn't change when you coast is classic wheel imbalance. A tire shop can balance the wheels quickly and cheaply.
Vibration only when accelerating, and not when coasting, points to the driveline: CV joints, driveshaft or engine mounts, not the wheels.
Shaking at all speeds points to a damaged tire (bulge or separated tread), a bent wheel or loose wheel nuts. Check the nuts and the tires right away.

documents.title: Clicking or popping noise when turning
keywords: clicking when turning the steering wheel
documents.overview: A repeated clicking or popping noise when turning, especially during tight turns while accelerating, is a classic sign of a worn outer CV (constant-velocity) joint on a front-wheel-drive or all-wheel-drive car. It is often caused by a torn CV boot that let the grease out and dirt in. Other parts can also make noises when turning, so it needs an inspection to confirm.
possible_causes: A worn outer CV joint, usually after its rubber boot has torn.
Worn wheel bearings, suspension joints or strut mounts.
Loose brake or suspension hardware, or something rubbing the wheel.
symptoms: Clicking that gets faster with speed in a tight turn; grease splattered around the inside of the wheel; vibration when accelerating can point to an inner CV joint.
checks: Look behind the front wheels for a torn rubber boot or grease spray, with the engine off and the car parked safely.
Note which side the noise comes from and whether it happens turning left, right or both.
professional_diagnostics: A technician inspects the CV boots and joints, wheel bearings and suspension and replaces the worn part.
documents.urgency: Have it inspected soon. A badly worn CV joint can fail and leave the car unable to drive; loud clunking or vibration when accelerating is more urgent.
needed_information: When the noise happens (turning, accelerating, over bumps), which side, and the vehicle's drive type.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Drive-axle and suspension service is vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: A clicking or popping noise when turning is most often a worn outer CV joint on a front-wheel-drive car, usually after its rubber boot has torn.
key_causes: a torn CV boot that let grease out and dirt in
actions: With the engine off, look behind the front wheels for a torn boot or grease sprayed around.
Have it inspected soon; a worn CV joint can break and cause loss of drive.
documents.drive_safety: For now, usually yes, but have it inspected soon. A worn CV joint can break and leave the car without drive.

documents.title: Battery or charging warning light while driving
keywords: battery light is on while driving
lights dim and the car stalled
documents.overview: A battery-shaped warning light while the engine is running usually means the charging system is not charging, most often a failing alternator, a broken or slipping drive belt, or a loose or corroded connection, rather than a bad battery. The car is then running on battery power alone and may stall when the battery runs down.
possible_causes: A failing alternator or voltage regulator.
A broken, loose or slipping drive belt.
Loose or corroded battery terminals or charging wires.
Less often, a battery fault.
symptoms: Dimming lights, electrical items working poorly, a whining or squealing belt noise, and on some engines a rising temperature if the same belt drives the water pump.
checks: Turn off non-essential electrical loads such as the radio and air conditioning.
If the temperature gauge rises or steering becomes heavy at the same time, the drive belt may have broken: stop when it is safe.
Drive only a short distance to a safe place or workshop; switching the engine off may mean it will not restart.
professional_diagnostics: A technician tests the battery, alternator output, belt and wiring before replacing parts.
documents.urgency: Prompt attention: arrange a charging-system check as soon as possible. Stop when it is safe if the temperature rises, steering becomes heavy or the car starts losing power.
needed_information: Whether other warning lights are on, any belt noise, and how the car behaves.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Warning-light meanings and required responses vary by vehicle.

documents.answer: A battery or charging light while driving means the charging system has a fault, usually an alternator that isn't charging, so the car is running on battery power and may stop.
key_causes: a broken or slipping drive belt
actions: Switch off electrical loads you don't need, such as the A/C, radio and heated seats.
documents.stop: Drive only as far as a safe place nearby, then stop; the car can lose power and stall when the battery runs down. If the temperature gauge also rises, stop straight away, because the same belt may drive the water pump.
documents.drive_safety: Only for a short distance. The car is running on battery power and can stall, so drive to a safe place nearby and have the charging system checked.

documents.title: Fluid leaking under the car: what the colour can suggest
keywords: water dripping from under the car
water under the car after using ac
documents.overview: The colour of a leak is a useful clue: clear water is usually A/C condensation, green, orange or pink can be coolant, brown or black is often engine oil, red can be transmission or power-steering fluid, and a clear-to-yellowish slippery fluid near a wheel can be brake fluid, and blue is usually windscreen-washer fluid.
possible_causes: Clear, odourless water near the front passenger side after using the air conditioning: usually normal condensation.
Green, orange or pink fluid with a sweet smell: coolant (antifreeze).
Brown or black oily fluid: engine oil.
Red or pink thin fluid: transmission fluid, or power-steering fluid on some vehicles.
Clear to brown slippery fluid near a wheel: possibly brake fluid, which is urgent.
Blue thin fluid: windshield washer fluid.
A strong gasoline or diesel smell: a fuel leak, which is a fire risk.
symptoms: A puddle or spots under the parked car, a falling fluid level, warning lights, overheating, or a change in how the brakes or steering feel.
checks: Place clean paper or cardboard under the car overnight to see the colour and where it drips.
Do not touch or taste unknown fluids, and keep children and pets away; coolant is poisonous.
Check fluid levels only when the engine is cold and as the owner's manual describes.
professional_diagnostics: A technician traces the leak to the hose, seal or component and checks the affected system.
documents.urgency: Do not drive if you suspect a brake-fluid or fuel leak, or if the brake pedal feels different: stop and arrange inspection or towing. Coolant and oil leaks need prompt repair before levels run low.
needed_information: Colour, smell and location of the leak, how much, and any warning lights.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Fluid types and colours vary by vehicle and brand.

documents.answer: The colour of a leak is a useful clue: clear water is usually A/C condensation, green, orange or pink can be coolant, brown or black is often engine oil, red can be transmission or power-steering fluid, and a clear-to-yellowish slippery fluid near a wheel can be brake fluid, and blue is usually windscreen-washer fluid.
actions: Put a light-coloured sheet under the car to see the colour and where it drips from.
documents.stop: A suspected brake-fluid or fuel leak means don't drive the car.

triage.ask: What colour is the fluid, and where under the car is it dripping?

answers.narrow: Green, pink or orange fluid near the front is coolant. Check the reservoir level and the hoses; don't drive far if the level keeps dropping.
Brown or black fluid under the engine is engine oil, from the oil pan, drain plug or a gasket. Check the dipstick; a slow seep can wait for a service, a fast drip can't.
Red fluid near the middle is usually transmission or power-steering fluid. Have it checked soon; low fluid damages the transmission.
Clear, odourless water under the front passenger side is normal A/C condensation.
Blue fluid is almost always windscreen-washer fluid from a cracked reservoir or hose. It's harmless to the engine; refill it and fix the leak when convenient.

documents.title: Flat tire or puncture
documents.overview: If a tire is flat or losing air, slow down, move to a safe place away from traffic, switch on the hazard lights and stop. Driving on a flat tire quickly destroys it and can damage the wheel and make the car hard to control.
possible_causes: A nail, screw or other object in the tread.
Damage from a pothole or kerb, including a cut or bulge in the sidewall.
A leaking valve or a poor seal between the tire and the rim.
symptoms: The car pulling to one side, a flapping or thumping noise, heavy steering, or a tire-pressure warning light.
checks: Stop on firm, level ground away from traffic before doing anything.
Use the spare tire or repair kit only as the owner's manual describes; a temporary spare has a speed and distance limit.
Do not drive on a tire with a sidewall cut or bulge.
professional_diagnostics: A tire shop checks whether a puncture in the tread can be repaired properly; sidewall damage usually means the tire must be replaced.
documents.urgency: Stop as soon as it is safe. If you are driving a rental vehicle, contact the rental team before arranging repairs.
needed_information: Where the damage is, whether a spare is fitted, and whether the warning light is on.

sources.name: Vehicle-specific owner's manual and service information
sources.reference: Spare-tire and repair-kit instructions are vehicle-specific.

documents.answer: If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire.
key_causes: a nail, screw or other object in the tread
a cut or bulge in the sidewall from a pothole or kerb
a poor seal between the tire and the rim
actions: Use the spare tire or repair kit as the owner's manual describes; a temporary spare has speed and distance limits.
If the sidewall is damaged or you can't change it safely, call roadside assistance. In a rental car, contact the rental team first.
documents.professional: A tire shop can tell whether a tread puncture can be repaired; sidewall damage usually means replacing the tire.
documents.drive_safety: No. Driving on a flat tire destroys it, can damage the wheel and makes the car harder to control; fit the spare or call roadside assistance.

documents.title: Steering is heavy or hard to turn
keywords: steering wheel is hard to turn
hard to turn the steering wheel
documents.overview: Steering that suddenly becomes heavy or hard to turn usually means the power-steering assistance is reduced or lost, or a tire problem is adding resistance. You can usually still steer, but it takes much more effort, which makes the car harder to control.
possible_causes: Low or under-inflated front tires, or a flat tire.
Hydraulic power steering: low or leaking power-steering fluid, a worn or slipping drive belt, or a failing pump.
Electric power steering: a fault in the steering motor, sensor or wiring, often with a steering warning light.
Worn or binding steering or suspension joints.

documents.title: What ABS (anti-lock braking) is and how it works
documents.answer: ABS stands for anti-lock braking system. In a hard stop it rapidly pulses the brakes on any wheel that is about to lock, so the tires keep grip and you can still steer while braking.
actions: In an emergency stop with ABS, press the brake pedal hard and keep pressing; a buzzing or pulsing pedal is normal and means ABS is working, so don't pump the brakes.
ABS doesn't always shorten stopping distances, especially on gravel or loose surfaces, so keep a safe distance.

documents.title: Power-steering (EPS) warning light
documents.answer: The EPS light means the electric power-steering system has a fault. The car can still be steered, but the steering may suddenly feel much heavier, especially at low speed and when parking.

an overheated power-steering motor after a lot of full-lock turning
a fault in the power-steering control unit
actions: Stop somewhere safe, switch the engine off, wait a minute and restart; if the light goes out it was often a temporary voltage fault, but have it checked.

documents.title: Signs of a weak or dying car battery
keywords: how do i know if my battery is dying
how do i know if my battery is weak
how to tell if battery is bad
documents.answer: The usual signs of a weak battery are slow or laboured cranking, especially in the morning, dim lights or a flickering dashboard when starting, clicking when you turn the key, and needing jump starts. A battery that is over about 3 years old in a hot climate is more likely to fail.
key_causes: age: most car batteries last about 2 to 4 years in a hot climate
short trips that never fully recharge the battery
a weak alternator that isn't charging it
actions: Have the battery load-tested at a battery shop or workshop; it takes a few minutes and shows whether it's weak.
Check the terminals are tight and free of white or green corrosion.

documents.title: Which engine oil type and grade to use
documents.answer: Use the oil grade (viscosity, such as 0W-20 or 5W-30) and the specification (such as API SP or ILSAC GF-6) listed in the owner's manual or on the oil filler cap. The grade matters more than the brand.
actions: Fully synthetic oil protects better in heat and stop-and-go traffic and is required by many newer engines; use it if the manual says so.
Diesel engines need oil rated for diesel (for example API CK-4 or the maker's specification), so don't swap gasoline and diesel oils unless the oil is rated for both.

documents.title: Car caught in a flood or driven through deep water
documents.answer: If the car has been in a flood, don't try to start it: water in the engine can bend internal parts the moment it turns over, and wet electrics can short. Have it towed and inspected first.
key_causes: water drawn into the engine through the air intake
water in the fuel, transmission or differential oil
wet wiring, connectors and control modules
wet brakes after driving through water
actions: Disconnect the battery if you can do it safely, and take photos of the water line inside and outside the car.
Have the engine oil, transmission fluid and fuel checked for water before the car is started.
If you drove through water and the car still runs, test the brakes gently at low speed until they dry and work normally.
documents.stop: Never drive into floodwater you can't see the bottom of; if water reaches the bottom of the doors, the engine can stall or the car can float. Don't start a car that was submerged.

documents.title: How to save fuel and improve fuel economy
documents.answer: The biggest savings come from how you drive: accelerate and brake smoothly, keep a steady speed, and avoid long idling. Keeping the tires at the correct pressure and the car serviced also helps.

Remove heavy items you don't need from the car, and use the A/C sensibly.
Keep to the service schedule: a clogged air filter or worn spark plugs waste fuel.

documents.title: When to replace tires
keywords: when should i replace my tires
documents.answer: Replace a tire when the tread is worn down to the wear bars (about 1.6 mm), when it has a bulge, a deep cut or cracks in the sidewall, or when it's more than about 5 to 6 years old even if the tread looks fine.
actions: Look for the small raised wear bars in the tread grooves; if the tread is level with them, the tire is worn out.
Check the 4-digit date code on the sidewall (for example 2321 means week 23 of 2021) to see the tire's age.
Replace tires in pairs on the same axle so grip stays even.
documents.stop: Don't drive on a tire with a bulge, a cut down to the cords, or worn-through tread; fit the spare.
